forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Durham highways overspent by £1.192m in 2025/26, driven by £3.334m on road defect repairs
news_drafts.lead:
Durham County Council's highways service overspent its day-to-day budget by £1.192m in 2025/26, according to a report to the Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee, which met on 2 October. Day-to-day spending (revenue spending) covers staff, services and contracts, as opposed to spending on things that last.

The report says the overspend was mainly due to £3.334m spent over budget on highways maintenance, specifically repairing defects in the road network. It describes this as "a recurring issue for several years". Where the work qualified, the council paid for £1.8m of the repairs as capital spending, which is money spent on things that last, such as roads. That left £1.534m of the defect repair overspend falling on the day-to-day budget.

For the structural gap in the highways budget, the council plans a new Land Rental Scheme, which the report says will start in 2026/27.

news_drafts.headline: Durham council implemented 97% of audit actions due by June; one Resources review rated limited
news_drafts.lead:
Durham County Council had carried out 392 of the 405 internal audit recommendations due by 30 June, or 97%, the Audit Committee was told at its meeting on 30 September. All 13 that missed their original dates have been given new ones, and none has missed the revised date.

The same quarterly report from Internal Audit, the team that checks the council's controls, records one review in the quarter with a limited assurance opinion, meaning controls were not reliably managing the risks identified. It was in the Resources service grouping, and the detail is in a confidential Part B paper. Unplanned staff absences meant the team delivered 723 productive days, 18% of the annual plan against the 22.5% expected for the quarter. The report says the service was back to full staffing by the start of the second quarter. A review of the Digital Durham Grant was dropped from the plan because there was no spend on the programme this year. The paper gives no reason.

The committee's annual report sets out the wider record. Forvis Mazars, the external auditor, gave an unqualified opinion (full sign-off) on the 2024/25 accounts and on the council's value for money arrangements on 26 November 2025. Internal Audit's overall opinion on the control environment for 2025/26 was "moderate". On 31 July the Corporate Director of Resources concluded the council has "a history of stable finance" and no significant risks to its continuing operation. A Local Government Association peer review in October 2025 called it "a financially well-managed and stable organisation", with debt and reserves "consistent with accepted sector practice".

The committee also heard from the Corporate Director of Children and Young People's Services on 27 February about rising Children in Care costs, including unregulated and crisis placements. On 26 March it held a special meeting on the governance, decision-making and value for money of the Toft Hill and High Etherley Bypass, focused on what lessons can be taken forward.

news_drafts.headline: County Durham's schools high needs overspend was £16.7m in 2025-26 against £14.25m budgeted
news_drafts.lead:
County Durham's spending on support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) overspent by £16.742m in 2025-26, the Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee was told on 25 September. The council had budgeted for a deficit of £14.250m on the high needs part of the dedicated schools grant (the government money that funds schools, with high needs covering children with SEND). The outturn, the actual figures once the year had ended, was £2.492m worse. The overall schools-funding deficit stood at £36.080m at the year end, up from £20.229m.

The papers attribute part of the overspend to alternative provision, which exceeded budget by £1.754m, and to post-16 independent and non-maintained special schools, which overspent by £0.830m because demand was higher than anticipated. For 2026-27, the council set the high needs budget with a deficit of £30.278m. The first-quarter forecast is £31.105m, or £0.827m higher, because of more special school places and higher costs for pupils with complex needs. On that forecast the cumulative deficit reaches £67.185m by 31 March 2027.

The council submitted its Local SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education in June 2026. Once the plan is assessed and approved, funding of up to 90% of the £36.080m deficit, or £32.472m, would be paid to the council, leaving about £3.6m. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off the main balance sheet, expires on 31 March 2028, when the paper says central government assumes responsibility for SEND funding.

findings.committee: Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: The Light leisure centre development reprofiled to 2026/27 opening, creating £0.392m underspend against operations budget
findings.detail: The Light was budgeted to open in 2025/26 but will now open in 2026/27. This created a £0.392m underspend against operations budgets in 2025/26. The capital development itself has been reprofiled with £1.188m slipping to 2026/27, indicating at least a one-year delay from the original plan.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to track whether high-profile capital projects are delivering to schedule, as slippage can indicate project management issues and tie up capital funding and working capital longer than planned.
findings.figures: £1.188m capital reprofiled to 2026/27; £0.392m operations budget underspend due to non-opening in 2025/26
findings.quote: £1.188 million reprofiled against The Light development and £0.392 million underspend against The Light operations budget due to the venue not opening until 202/27.

findings.committee: Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility grant now embedded in core waste revenue budgets for 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: Strategic Waste achieved a £4.805m underspend in 2025/26 by using the Extended Producer Responsibility grant to offset core spending. Of this, £3.891m has been set aside in earmarked reserves for future commitments on food waste recycling. The council has explicitly 'built into the 2026/27 and 2027/28 revenue budgets' the use of EPR grant funding to offset core service costs.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand that core waste service budgets now depend on continued EPR grant receipt through 2027/28. Any reduction or cessation of EPR funding would require budget rebalancing or service reduction.
findings.figures: £4.805m Strategic Waste underspend; £3.891m set aside in EPR reserve; EPR funding embedded in 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets
findings.quote: The use of the EPR grant to fund core activity has been built into the 2026/27 and 2027/28 revenue budgets as part of the approved budget and MTFP(16) report agreed by County Council on 18 February 2026.

findings.committee: Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Whorlton Suspension Bridge and Wolsingham Bridge repairs require combined £1.352m budget uplifts due to survey inadequacies and inflation
findings.detail: Whorlton Suspension Bridge overspent by £1.024m due to delays in quantifying remedial works required and rising inflation, with issues on progress milestones involving Historic England and the Environment Agency. Wolsingham Bridge overspent by £0.328m because initial surveys did not identify the extent of damage to the bridge deck and waterproofing. Both overruns were funded from corporate capital contingencies and internal transfers.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand the council's asset condition survey and capital planning process, particularly where survey failures have led to cost escalation, and whether rising inflation is creating cascading pressures across the capital programme.
findings.figures: Whorlton Suspension Bridge £1.024m overspend; Wolsingham Bridge £0.328m overspend; combined £1.352m
findings.quote: £1.024 million overspend on Whorlton Suspension Bridge, which now requires a budget uplift due to delays to quantify the full scale of the remedial works required and rising inflation, arising from issues on progress milestones with Historic England and the Environment Agency. £0.328 million overspend on Wolsingham Bridge due to initial surveys from principal inspections not showing the extent of severe damage to the bridge deck and waterproofing when resurfacing was removed.

findings.committee: Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Transport capital programme £7.306m underspent (27% of budget) reprofiled to 2026/27 due to procurement delays and utility coordination issues
findings.detail: Transport and Contracted Services capital underspent by £7.306m against a revised £26.837m budget, with variances driven by City Region Sustainable Transport Settlement procurement delays (£2.581m), Towns Deal Programme utility coordination delays (£0.899m), Bus Service Improvement Plan delays (£0.910m), and multiple other schemes delayed by utility diversions and contract completions. All have been reprofiled to 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether concurrent delays across multiple transport programmes indicate delivery capability constraints within the council or its supply chain that could affect future project timescales and funding drawdown patterns.
findings.figures: £7.306m capital underspend (27% of £26.837m budget); £2.581m CRSTS; £0.899m Towns Deal; £0.910m Bus Service Improvement Plan
findings.quote: Project spend of £2.581 million within City Region Sustainable Transport Settlement (CRSTS), has been reprofiled to 2026/27. Delays are due to procurement processes with the Bowburn Development Route, with one contract having been recently awarded.

findings.committee: Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Car parking income fell £0.404m short of MTFP(14) savings targets, with mitigation still under development
findings.detail: Noses Point and Crimdon car parks underachieved income by £0.404m against budget. These shortfalls were embedded in MTFP(14) savings assumptions but have not materialized. The service acknowledges it is still 'developing mitigating actions' to balance the 2026/27 budget, suggesting the issue has not yet been resolved.
findings.matters: A finance director tracking savings delivery would want to know whether planned income shortfalls indicate a structural change in parking demand that will affect future years' budgeting assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.404m underachieved car parking income at Noses Point and Crimdon
findings.quote: £0.404 million underachieved car parking income at Noses Point and Crimdon which were MTFP(14) savings factored into the 2024/25 budget and where income has fallen short of the MTFP savings forecasts. Mitigating actions are being developed by the service to ensure that there is a balanced budget set for 2026/27.
